growth_story.headline: Angola's post-war oil boom lifted income per person, but lower oil prices and shrinking oil output since 2014 have left it 25.2 percent below its peak.
growth_story.arc: In the war years of the 1990s, income per person fell by 2.0 percent a year over 1990–2000, with a drop of 26.4 percent in 1993 alone. After the long civil war ended, rising oil output, high oil prices and oil-backed loans drove a boom, and income per person grew 6.4 percent a year over 2001–2008. Growth then stalled at -0.2 percent a year over 2009–2016: income per person peaked in 2014, and falling world oil prices, maturing oil fields and lower oil investment tipped the economy into recession. Since 2017 income per person has shrunk by 2.4 percent a year, with the worst year in 2020 at -8.3 percent as the COVID-19 pandemic deepened the slump. By 2025 it was still 25.2 percent below its 2014 peak and lower than in 1980, the first year of the record.

threads.title: Oil boom after the war
threads.text: Once the civil war was over, rising oil output, high oil prices and loans backed by oil drove fast growth and helped pay for the post-war years. The World Bank notes that the oil money did not build the infrastructure, skills or institutions that other industries needed.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe strong growth from 2004 to 2014 and a recovery in 2024, but these are figures for the whole economy. In the data, income per person stalled from 2009 (an average of -0.2 percent a year over 2009–2016) and grew only 1.8 percent in 2024 and 0.1 percent in 2025, because the population grows almost as fast as output. The World Bank's October 2026 outlook also puts the gap from the 2014 level deeper than the 25.2 percent in this data, likely because it measures income in local currency rather than in dollars.
